text: Is the sentence "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" spoken by a human speaker to a human listener?
Is the speaker a machine or artificial intelligence (rather than a living biological being)?
Is the speaker an animal (such as a pet parrot)?
Is the repeated sentence something that is written or displayed (for example on a sign, page, or screen) rather than spoken aloud?
Is the written sentence addressed to the narrator personally — that is, written by someone for the narrator to read — rather than being generic printed text like a label, notice, or warning?
Is the narrator being made to write or copy the sentence repeatedly as a punishment or imposed task?
Did the narrator write these seven copies of the sentence themselves?
Is the person whom the narrator wrote all seven copies to read a romantic partner or former romantic partner?
Were the seven copies written on seven separate occasions or separate items (such as seven different notes or messages), rather than all written together on one single surface?
Is the romantic partner now dead (deceased)?
Did the narrator cause or contribute to the partner's death?

In the story, does the sentence express the dead partner's own feelings toward the narrator — i.e., the partner is the one who was disappointed and who was "never coming back" — rather than being the narrator's message to the partner?
Did the romantic partner die by suicide (taking their own life)?
Did the narrator write these messages as part of a cover-up — to make others believe the partner left voluntarily (that the partner is the one who went away)?
Is the narrator's "trouble" that the staged notes are in the narrator's own handwriting, revealing the deception?
Was the partner's death caused by the narrator deliberately (an intentional killing), rather than an unintentional accident that the narrator then concealed?

Were these notes intended to be mistaken for the dead partner's own handwriting — i.e., a forged farewell note supposedly written by the partner saying "I'm never coming back" — so that people would think the partner walked out?

The narrator deliberately murdered their romantic partner. To hide the killing, the narrator forged a farewell note in the partner's voice — "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — so that friends, family, or police would believe the partner had simply walked out and left of their own accord. The narrator wrote this same forged message out seven times (repeatedly copying/practicing it) to make the deception convincing.

The plan fatally backfires: the staged notes are in the narrator's own handwriting, not the dead partner's, so the forgery itself gives the narrator away. The repeated line looks like the partner's words but was in fact written by the narrator — not the partner's true feelings at all. Realizing the forged note now exposes rather than conceals the murder, the narrator sighs, "I know I'm in trouble."

Is the reason the sentence appears seven times that the narrator wrote it compulsively or obsessively (for example, filling a page in distress), rather than deliberately producing several separate copies for the cover-up?
Is the flaw in the cover-up simply that the forged notes were written in the narrator's ordinary, undisguised handwriting — the narrator made no real attempt to imitate or conceal it?
Were the seven repeated lines written as handwriting samples for an investigation — for example, dictated to the narrator by police to compare with the forged note?
Is the narrator a child or teenager?
Was the partner actually leaving or breaking up with the narrator (about to go) at the time the narrator killed them?
Did the narrator copy the sentence from a real message or note that the partner had previously written or sent to the narrator, using it as the model for the forgery?
Could the dead partner not have written any note themselves — for example because they were illiterate, blind, or physically unable to write?
Was the partner illiterate — unable to read and write at all?
Was the dead partner blind (unable to see)?
Was the partner physically unable to write because of a problem with their hands or arms (for example, no hands, paralysis, or a hand injury)?

The narrator deliberately murdered their romantic partner. To cover it up, the narrator hand-wrote a farewell message in the partner's voice — "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — so that others would believe the partner had simply walked out and left of their own accord, rather than having been killed. The narrator wrote this same line out seven times.

The deception is undone by the writing itself: the forged note is in the narrator's own handwriting, and the dead partner never wrote it. So the staged "farewell" instead points straight back at the narrator as the forger and killer. Realizing the note exposes rather than protects them, the narrator says, "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."
Did the forged note purport to be written by the partner and addressed to the narrator (a goodbye/breakup note the partner supposedly left for the narrator)?
Is the narrator's "trouble" external — the fear or fact of being caught and punished by other people — rather than purely internal guilt or conscience?

Was the very repetition itself — the same sentence appearing seven identical times, which is implausible for someone genuinely leaving — one of the things that made the forgery look staged and suspicious?
Is the partner non-human (a non-human entity, such as an imaginary being, a spirit, or an object)?
Did the narrator conceal or dispose of the partner's body (for example, hide, bury, or otherwise get rid of it)?

The narrator deliberately killed their romantic partner. To make it appear the partner had left of their own accord, the narrator forged a farewell note saying "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — presenting it as the partner's goodbye so that others would believe the partner had walked out voluntarily rather than been killed.

The narrator wrote the message out repeatedly, and the forgery fails on the one point that matters: the writing is in the narrator's own hand, not the partner's. The note the partner supposedly left therefore betrays the person who actually wrote it. Because the staged farewell exposes the narrator as the forger and killer, the narrator understands they will be caught and punished by others: "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."
Was the forged farewell note intended to make the narrator appear as the innocent, abandoned victim — the one who was left — rather than simply to conceal that a killing had occurred?
Did the deception initially succeed — did other people at first believe the partner had simply left — before it was exposed?
Did the narrator lead others to believe the partner was still alive and had gone away, when in fact the partner was already dead?
Was the forged note ostensibly written at a time when the partner was, in fact, already dead — i.e., it was supposedly the partner's note from a time they could no longer have written anything?
Is the narrator composing this very account — the repeated lines plus the sigh — as a written statement or confession, after already being caught?
Did the discovery of the partner's body/remains reveal that they had died before the farewell note was supposedly written?

The narrator deliberately killed their romantic partner. To make people believe the partner was still alive and had simply walked out, the narrator forged a farewell note in the partner's name: "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back." The narrator wrote this same message out repeatedly, in an attempt to reproduce the partner's writing and pass the note off as theirs.

The forgery defeats itself in two ways. The handwriting is actually the narrator's own — the imitation failed — and, more damningly, the note purports to be the partner's words from a time when the partner was already dead, so the partner could not possibly have written it. The staged departure is therefore exposed as a fiction, revealing that the partner never left but was killed. Because this evidence now points to the narrator, they know they will be caught and punished: "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."
Did the narrator write the note(s) before killing the partner — intending to use them afterwards as an alibi — rather than writing them after the killing?

Were the note's words originally the narrator's own message of disappointment and departure toward the partner (the narrator being the one who was disappointed and leaving), which the narrator later repurposed to explain the partner's disappearance?
Did the narrator write these seven copies of the sentence on the same day/at the same time the death was being covered up (i.e., as part of the staging itself), rather than at some later date?
Did the forged note present the partner as having gone away to a specific place or with a specific person (an elopement or relocation), rather than merely ending the relationship with the narrator?
When producing the note, did the narrator deliberately attempt to copy or mimic the dead partner's handwriting?

Was the crucial giveaway that imitating the partner's handwriting was impossible or pointless in the circumstances — specifically, that the act of writing the message in the partner's hand could only have been done by someone else, because the message's own wording/format gave it away as the narrator's composition?

Did the narrator kill the partner through direct physical violence (hands or a weapon), rather than by deliberately causing the death indirectly — for example, by abandoning or neglecting the partner in circumstances that killed them?
Has the narrator already been accused or taken into custody?
Beyond this note, did the narrator fabricate additional evidence (for example, other messages or records) to support the story that the partner was alive and had left?

Was the repeated sentence written by the narrator as the words the partner supposedly left behind — i.e., the narrator wrote the same farewell message over and over to pass it off as the dead partner's parting words?
Does the exposure of the forged note, by itself, indicate that the partner is dead (rather than only showing that the story of the partner leaving is false)?

The narrator deliberately killed their romantic partner. To make other people believe the partner was still alive and had simply gone away, the narrator wrote out the partner's supposed parting words — "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — over and over, trying to pass them off as the dead partner's own farewell by imitating the partner's handwriting, and doing this as part of staging the cover-up.

The fabrication collapses on its own details. The writing is in the narrator's own hand, and the note is presented as the partner's words from a time when the partner was already dead — so the partner could not have written it. That exposes the "partner left" story as a fake, not a proof of anything else, and the narrator knows the suspicion will now fall on them: "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."
Did the narrator have no genuine specimen of the partner's handwriting to imitate?
Were the seven written copies made on official documents or forms (for example as signatures or entries), rather than in a letter or note?
According to the forged note's own story, is the partner the disappointed party who is leaving the narrator — that is, does the note read as a message from the partner to the narrator?

Was the narrator's imitation attempt undone specifically because the same message written many times by one hand made the writing's true author obvious — the repetition betraying a single writer at work rather than a genuine note?

Note: host already answered "no" to repetition being suspicious/staged-looking, so I'm not re-asking that framed claim; I'm testing whether the *single-author uniformity across the copies* is what exposed it.

Is the reason the note "could not have been written by the partner" something visible in the note itself — such as the words naming a thing/event/situation that only existed (or only happened) after the partner's death?

That's my one remaining discriminator: whether the anachronism is internal to the text (a reference the dead partner couldn't have known) rather than merely the note's date relative to the death.
Is the narrator's trouble that they must now account for, or produce, the partner they claimed had left — which they cannot do, because the partner is actually dead?
Are the seven written copies still in the narrator's own possession (or were they written for the narrator's own use), rather than having been given or left for other people to find?

Is the narrator keeping the seven copies for the purpose of practising/perfuming the imitation until it looks convincing enough to be passed off as the partner's writing?

My check: possession = yes means the copies are drafts in the narrator's hands, so the "cover-up" is at the preparation stage. I want one confirmation that the seven are drafts of a single intended forgery before we submit, rather than something the narrator wrote purely to reassure themselves.

To cover it, they set about making people believe the partner was still alive and had simply left, by forging the partner's own departure message — "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — written in imitation of the partner's handwriting. The seven copies are the narrator's practice drafts, written for their own use and still in their own possession; none was ever handed over or planted for others to find.

The plan is unsalvageable, and the narrator sees it: no matter how many times it is rehearsed, the hand remains the narrator's own and not the partner's, and the note would have to be the partner's words from a time when the partner was already dead, so the partner could not have written it. The pretence cannot hold, and the narrator knows the consequence falls on them: "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."

Was there a specific outside event (for example, someone visiting, asking about the partner, or growing suspicious) that made the narrator realize they were in trouble, rather than only their own reflection on the drafts?
Is the decisive fatal flaw of the forged note its timing — that it would have to be the partner's words from a time when the partner was already dead?

The seven copies are the narrator's practice drafts, made for their own use and still in their own possession; nothing was ever handed over or planted for anyone to find.

Sitting alone with these drafts, the narrator sees that the imitation cannot pass as the partner's and that the consequence therefore falls on them: "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble."
In the drafts, does the writing actually resemble the partner's handwriting (the imitation succeeding), rather than resembling the narrator's own normal handwriting?
Does the narrator still intend to complete and eventually use the forged note, rather than having abandoned the plan?

Is the fatal flaw in the note's wording or phrasing (the way it is expressed betraying the narrator), rather than in its handwriting?

Is the narrator's trouble that these kept practice drafts are themselves incriminating evidence — they sit in the narrator's own possession, in the narrator's own hand, and will be found and show who wrote the "partner's" note?
Is the finished forged note meant to be shown to a reader who would recognize the narrator's own handwriting (for example, someone close to the narrator, or to both of them)?
